Still brooding over the photos he'd gathered from his last case, Ted Green, private investigator, sat at his desk with a half empty bottle of scotch and an empty highball glass, when the mail slot opened, and a plain manilla envelope dropped in with an ominous clang in the mail basket. It was late, too late for the post to be arriving. What could it be?

Half drunk, Ted pulled himself out of his office chair and stumbled over to the door. Picking up envelope, which was inordinately heavy, he stumbled back to his desk. Inspecting the bloated envelope, it was plain except for the hand-written name on it, "Det. Green".

Ted felt the package clumsily. It had something rectangular in it. Bemused, he tore the envelop open with disregard. Inside was a small cardboard box. "Why not just address the box," Ted thought to himself. Through the haze of a pint or more of scotch, Ted didn't think much of the odd packaging. He slid the top of the box off, and inside he was surprised to find a single, severed human finger.

Shocked, Ted dropped the box and pushed his chair away from his desk, knocking over the half empty bottle of scotch in the process.

"What the hell?!?" Ted exclaimed with obvious surprise.

Questions began to stream through his head. All of the typical questions, "who, why, when, etc..."

Upon closer inspection, there were no obvious answers. Ted's mind raced. He lit a cigarette and looked on with a mix of curiosity and terror at the finger. It lay on a bed of cotten-balls, and appeared 'fresh'. "Who's could it be," he wondered.

A sense of dread swept over the normally stoic private investigator. The finger was clearly female; it was carefully manicured, obviously from a lady of means. The dread in his mind turned to knots in his stomach. "Could this be one of Beverley's fingers," he wondered.

Beverley had been a client who had hired him a couple of months ago to find out who her husband was having an affair with. What Mrs. Salsiccia had failed to mention when she retained Green's services was that Mr. Salsiccia was in fact a cappo with one of the local mobsters. Ted had discovered this little fact the "hard" way, when some of Salsiccia's boys had confiscated his brownie and roughed him up.

"But why now," wondered the detective.

Green thumbed through a small notebook, nervously looking for the phone number Mrs. Salsiccia had left for him, and picked-up the receiver of his telephone. "Operator," he began, "connect me to 72-4313 please."

Green's stomach began to heave the more the phone rang. No one picked-up. Just as he was about to hang-up, after twelve rings or so, a man answered gruffly, "Hello?"

Despite having talked to Mrs. Salsiccia numerous times by phone, a man had never answered. Panicked, Green placed the receiver back on the hook and leaned back in his chair.

"This is no good," he said outloud, to no one.

Green picked-up the spilled bottle and poured another glass, which he quickly threw back in a single swallow.

Rising slowly from his chair, Ted pulled his coat and hat from the rack in the corner, and meandered towards the door. "Time to take a look in person, I suppose," he said out-loud to himself as he staggered to the door.

He never made it to the door though, as the last double shot of scotch hit him, he barely made it to the leather couch he too often slept on, his hat falling quietly to the floor. He'd have to deal with this tomorrow, when he was sober.

There was a storm brewing outside.

There was a faint electricity in the air, it might have just been the brewing storm, but it set my teeth on edge like nails down a blackboard

My flat was dark, the clouds had come over quickly, blanketing the city in their shadow.

I sighed as I turned on the halogen light, it coughed and spluttered it's brightness on my meager belonging before the light finally took.

This flat is all I have left, and even then how long I get to keep it was still in the air.

There was a thud.

That was strange, did something fall?

I walked to the hallway to see everything on the table where I left it.

Where did that sound come from then? Was it the kitchen? Was it someone in another flat? I could even have been the

Post.

There was a letter in the cage.

It was blank save the address of the flat, and my name: Lewis Cooper.

That's my old name.

That's my old name!

I stagger backwards as my balance momentarily fails. My mouth turns dry, it seemed like the water was needed for my pores, I was already dripping with cold sweat.

How did they know that name?

How long ago did that name die?

17 years ago the ship sank, everyone died.

Then Mark washed up on the shore.

But this said Lewis.

I took the letter and returned to the sofa. The TV was babbling about the most recent 'victory', I turned it off.

The letter had an ominous weight to it.

Would the words it bore carry the same weight?

My hands were shaking as I tried to open the letter, it was as if they were resisting my commands to them as they fumbled at the envelope.

Who would know, the fake records were perfect.

My mind raced to make connections, neurons firing as the panic spread.

There was little inside.

Two words that would crush this life I had made for myself. Written on a piece of thick paper, a faint military watermark visible.

We know.

With that was a dog tag, corroded from years at the bottom of the ocean, the number as familiar as the back of my hand: 469910. My military conscription number. Below it my name, my real name, the name I had deserted when I deserted my post that day. When I ran to the lifeboat not the guns. When I lived while others died.

My mind stopped racing, my panic subsided, a strange calm washed over me as one thought filled my mind.

It's over.

Calm was the wrong word, this wasn't acceptance, this was surrender.

My body felt like lead, my hand dropped, the letter falling to join the debris on the floor. I slumped in the sofa, crushed by the weight of 2 short words.

Thunder cackled outside.

The warm rain thudded against the windows causing steam to rise as the large drops touched the cool glass. The gentle beat of the rain lulled Sylvia into relaxation. Kicking off her tired, black heels, she poured herself a glass of dry Riesling. She stretched, her trim body’s shadow dancing against the flame of the crackling fireplace. She stripped from her boysenberry dress, tossing it on the floor, changing into her silky black pajamas. She let down her long, dark curls, and wiped away her make-up. The office party hadn’t been awful, but she was glad to be home.

Sylvia sunk into her chair, slowly putting her aching feet on the wooden coffee table. She pulled the blanket close, covering her legs in its soft warmth. The rain pitter-pattered slightly harder against the sides of the small house; the low rumbles of thunder were just soft enough to not break her concentration as she focused on a book. Sylvia took a long sip of wine. Her body relaxed; her aching feet slowly dissipated to a solid beat of content.

A few hazy hours passed, the bottle half empty by now. She heard some scuffling outside.

Just the raccoons she thought to herself, getting up from her cozy chair. Water seeped in from the open window; she supposed she’d forgotten to close it. Shutting the window, she stretched again. He bones cracked, the familiar jolts of popping sensations overwhelming her. She had figured it had been three hours since she last moved. Her cat walked over, brushing against her legs. She leaned over and pet him, picking the small creature up in her arms. She walked back to the chair and sat, the cat softly purring in her lap. His rhythmic purring could be felt through her chest. Like a tiny humming, it eased her. She closed her heavy eyes, wine and tiredness made her want to go to sleep.

THUD

She looked up, the cat jumped. Her heart thudded against her chest, a sudden start in the dead of night. It sounded like mail had come.

At this hour? she walked over to the mail bin. Surely enough, a large white envelope. The thunder crashed. She jumped, a lump growing in her throat. She looked at the envelope.

Sylvia T. Grant

Nothing else was on the envelope. She shook her head, trying to rid herself of the tiny electric feelings of panic going through her small body. She tossed it on the counter, hoping to just ignore it until tomorrow. She got to the kitchen, pouring herself another glass of wine. It was then she realized there was no postage on the envelope.

Gathering her glass, the cat now comfortably curled up by the fire, she walked to the table. Studying the envelope again, she noticed not even her address was on the envelope.

She shook.

Her throat seemed to close around her, the dizzying effect making her tremble.

Probably just a neighbor. Nothing to worry about. She shivered slightly, goosebumps covering her body as a cold chill went down her back. As her hands shook, she opened the envelope. It contained three items.

Sylvia’s eyes grew wide as a look of pure terror crossed her face. The hair on the back of her neck stood up, her knees weak, she leaned against the table.

It was a polaroid of her. Just hours ago. Stretching in her boysenberry dress. The next polaroid was of her, sitting in her chair, reading. Tingling filled her hands, unable to move with precision, the last item, a handwritten letter, violently shook in her hands. The terror taking over, her eyes darted to any moving shadow. She placed the letter on the table.

“My dear, I noticed you at the party. I’m quite comfortable here. Your security is rather lacking. No worries, my precious darling. You’ll be with me soon enough.”

It was her own stationery. Written in her purple pen. Someone was inside her home.

The lights flickered. The firelight went out. Her breathing sharpened. Each breath she took stung like daggers, cutting into her sides. She ran to her bedroom, her footsteps echoing down the empty hallway. She curled up against her bed, each wave of terror clawing and peeling away at her skin.

Sylvia reached for the closest thing she had, a gun. Her chest hurt. Her ears thudded against her heartbeat. She couldn’t hear the rain, nor the thunder - but she heard the floorboards creak. Trembling, she aimed the gun in the direction of a shadow. The numbness taking over her mind, her head felt heavy, her eyes focused on a shadow.

“Oh. Don’t even bother with that.” a voice said from the darkness. It chuckled. She felt the ice cold hands press against her bare neck.

Sylvia pulled the trigger.

It's noon on a Sunday, suns beamin' down hot as can be, and I've just got home from church. Wife passed on last year, kids are all growed up and on their own. There's a thump at the front door.

I get up and walk over and there it is, a letter. All it says on it is my name, Richard. Huh. Shouldn't be gettin mail on a Sunday. Ain't right to make people work on the Lord's day, what's this all coming to. Hmm, no stamp. Hand delivered then? I pull it open.

"My dear Richard,

It's been a little over a year since we last saw each other, and I know you must be feeling lonely. You may be telling yourself you're too old to go find someone new, but you're only 52. The kids are gone, and I don't want you staying by yourself. Please get out of the house. I know that tramp Chelsea is still interested in you. Yes, I knew about her, but I know that you honored our marriage. You're free now, and it just pains me to see you sitting in the house all day. You rarely smoke your pipe anymore, and I just want you to enjoy life.

With love,

Eleanor"

Well, that's mighty strange. First time I've received a hand written letter from my wife. Must be one of the neighborhood kids playing a joke of some sort. Ain't no harm in it.

A week passes. Sunday, promptly at noon, another letter arrives.

"Richard,

This is not a joke being put on by a kid, this is your wife. If you don't get your sorry butt out of that chair next weekend, I will have some stern words for you.

-E"

Now this is mighty confusing. I turn the paper over and grab a pen.

"Eleanor,

I'm going to take your word and believe it is you. I will be out and about on Saturday. Please don't be mad. Hope the weather is nice up there.

Richard"

the stead rumble of the space stations systems shook his whiskey glass in tiny ripples. that wasn't normally a problem, but he and his investigation business, had been so cheap and, economically unlucky, that when he'd docked on the odinSS, he'd rented a space directly next to the ventilation section. his room was tiny and cramped, and filled with an extra dose of thick metal support beam decor.

he looked up as the mail slot made a noise, which it rarely did. he sat up from the stool that sat behind the white, round-bent shape of his desk. his desktop was floating off the table in hologram shapes. and he sunk it all back into the smart surface with a gesture. when he looked into the basket, the package was just a brown big envelope, but one from real paper, so it cost roughly 4 months of his own earnings. sitting down again, he opened it to find, ornate, golf filigreed real paper.

reading it, he was struck odd at first, then he bolted from his chair, swinging open the door and looking both ways down the corridor. it was empty, and the clear layer of the stations windows, showed earth rotating slowly below. he'd tried extremely hard to cut the ties to his past, that had forced him into planetary exile. and, it looked like he was no longer successful in that.

I can feel my eyebrows clawing downward and towards one another in frustration even before my brain registers the sound hitting my ears.

My eyes peel away from the pages in front of me and the glass of whiskey in my right hand throttles the small lamp table making the whiskey inside cling desperately to the walls before spilling slightly. I barely even notice my hand is wet as I get up to check the large bay window across the room. It was a stupid idea anyway considering how late it is but there is nothing but stray streetlamp light coming in through the window and even though I can't see it I'm pretty sure dark clouds are blocking out the sky.

I knew this was coming the moment I made my decision earlier today I just hadn't expected it to be so soon. I can feel my shoulders sag as my breath slowly escapes my lungs. "Ahh fuck," I tell myself as I reluctantly shuffle out of the study and into the hallway that leads to the front door.

I can just make out the small rectangle on the floor near the front door before my foot lands sideways on a half upturned bowl I had forgotten about. I struggle to right myself but my bathrobe clings to my legs and I brace for impact as I watch the floor rush towards me. Part of me wishes I wasn't such a clumsy bastard all the time and the other part of me is just glad I set down that glass of whiskey.

It only takes me a minute or two to catch my breath but its already too late. I can hear small yips coming from my spare bedroom and I know it'll be at least half an hour before I can get back to my book and whiskey. I peal myself up and off the floor and finally reach the end of the hallway. My hand snatches the envelope up quick and I can finally make out the letters on the front, Homeowners Association: Urgent Matter, Why in the hell did I move into this neighborhood is all I can think but I already know the reasons and slowly rip the envelope open to read its contents.

"Dear Homeowner,

We are aware that earlier today you purchased and brought home a pet, the breed of which is designated under the PROHIBITED section of the Homeowners Association Guide Book regarding pets.

It is of course upsetting to hear that you didn't involve us in this decision or at least discuss it with us prior to your actions. We have agreed to have a small assembly tomorrow evening in order to discuss the issue.

Your appearance would be much appreciated. We will see you around 6 pm.

Regards,

Your Local HOA"

I finish reading the letter as I reach the kennel in the spare bedroom. I squat down to unlock the front gate and out pops a whopping 7 pound terror of a pit bull. He jumps up on my knee as best he can and makes his best attempt to lick my face.

I put his leash on and walk him out the back patio onto the wet grass with the letter still in my hand. My shoulders start to sag again and thoughts of that glass in my study swirl slowly in my head. Guess I'll deal with these people tomorrow... at least by then I'll have the book the pound recommended finished.
